analysis.one_liner: Lets people delete their personal data from every data broker with a single request.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 2025 with a Republican sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors, then referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The DELETE Act targets data brokers: companies that buy and sell personal information about people they have no direct relationship with. It would require every data broker to register annually with the Federal Trade Commission and publicly disclose what data it collects, where it gets it, and how to opt out. The FTC would build a central system where a person fills out one free form and every registered broker must delete that person's data and stop collecting it. Brokers would have to check the registry at least every 31 days, delete matching records within 31 days, report their completion rates, and undergo an independent audit every three years. The FTC would enforce the rules under its existing authority against unfair and deceptive practices.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose personal information — addresses, phone numbers, browsing history, health and financial details — is bought and sold by brokers they have never dealt with. Anyone who wants to opt out of the data-trading economy could do it in one step instead of hunting down dozens of separate brokers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose personal data is traded

how_it_helps.text: A single, free online request through an FTC-run website would trigger deletion of the requester's personal information across every registered data broker, and stop future collection unless the person says otherwise.

Data brokers would have to register with the FTC each year and the FTC would publish their contact information, opt-out methods, and standardized answers about what data they collect and where it comes from in a downloadable, machine-readable format.
The system would store requests in salted, hashed registries so brokers query coded values rather than receiving lists of raw names and emails, and only registered brokers could query the registries.

Brokers would have to delete matching records within 31 days of a registry check, file annual reports on completion rates, and undergo an independent third-party compliance audit every three years, with records kept six years.
The FTC would enforce violations the same way it enforces unfair or deceptive practices, with its full existing powers and penalties.
State privacy laws that give people stronger protection than this bill would remain in effect; the bill preempts only inconsistent state rules.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the marketing ecosystem built on their data. The bill is free for individuals; its operating costs are capped at fees brokers pay the FTC. Brokers lose the ability to sell information about anyone who opts out, and the exclusions limit which parts of the industry are covered.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts several categories of data activity, including fraud prevention and identity verification, consumer reporting agencies, news organizations, and firms selling publicly available information used in connection with a person's business or profession, so a meaningful slice of broker activity falls outside the deletion right.

The FTC itself would hold hashed identifiers for everyone who opts in, creating a new database of registrants; the bill acknowledges the FTC cannot confirm the accuracy of broker responses and warns individuals they contact brokers at their own risk.

There is no private right of action in the bill: individuals cannot sue a broker that fails to delete their data. Enforcement depends entirely on FTC rulemaking, its annual completion-rate reports from brokers, and periodic audits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who opt in, this would be a real, practical remedy for a problem that today requires dozens of separate, often ignored opt-out requests. The design is thoughtful about security — hashed registries, no fee, ongoing audits — but the carve-outs for fraud-prevention and business-use data, the lack of any right to sue, and the security of the FTC's own registry are genuine limits. It is a meaningful fix with real gaps, not a total solution.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it so far this Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on April 3, 2025, on behalf of himself, Sen. Jon Ossoff, and Sen. Ben Ray Luján.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced.
Three cosponsors, all Democrats, have signed on.
No committee markup, vote, or floor action appears in the action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the data-trading market, which keep operating under today's rules while the bill sits without a scheduled vote; no one has gained new deletion rights yet.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named its top cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Jon Ossoff and Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside its Republican sponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: The bill has sat in committee since its April 2025 referral with no markup or vote scheduled.

against.name: Data broker industry
against.role: Companies whose business is buying and selling personal information
against.what_they_did: A mandatory deletion registry strikes at the core of this industry's business model; industry opposition to deletion mandates is widely reported, though nothing appears on the congressional record in this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred. The bill's only record of support is bipartisan: a Republican sponsor with three Democratic cosponsors, with no recorded opposition so far.

industries.note: These companies profit by compiling and selling personal information about people they have no relationship with. The bill would force annual registration, public disclosure of their practices, and mass deletion for anyone who requests it — removing their raw material for opt-in individuals.
Marketers buy targeting data through brokers. If people opt out at scale, the audience data behind much targeted advertising shrinks.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies, fraud-prevention and identity-verification firms
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes them from the definition of data broker, so they keep compiling and sharing personal information even after it would be deleted elsewhere — a carve-out some supporters accepted to keep the bill moving.

analysis.trajectory: A nearly identical DELETE Act passed the House in the previous Congress before dying in the Senate, and the reintroduced bill has bipartisan sponsorship. But it has sat in the Commerce Committee for months with no markup scheduled, and Senate bills that go this long without a committee vote rarely reach the floor. Privacy legislation sometimes moves late in a Congress, so it is not dead — the realistic path is waiting for the committee to act or folding the idea into a broader privacy bill.
